common_name: Jeri Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Clear Blue Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall so roots establish before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: Jeri is a Mary Dunn introduction prized for its heavily ruffled, clear medium-blue flowers with a crisp white signal, carried on well-branched stalks in mid-spring. It became a favorite parent plant in Louisiana iris breeding programs for passing on strong ruffling and clean color to its seedlings, and remains a dependable garden performer in its own right. Plant rhizomes shallowly in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade. Keep the planting evenly damp through the growing season and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to sustain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Clasped Hands Louisiana Iris (Unusual-Form White and Violet-Blue Bicolor)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall so roots establish before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: Clasped Hands is a distinctive M.D. Faith introduction noted for its unusual flower form: the narrow, upright standards fold and interlock above the flaring violet-blue falls in a way that gives the cultivar its name, set off by a bold white-edged signal. This DeBaillon Medal-winning cultivar draws attention in the spring border for its novelty as much as its color, and it has been used by hybridizers seeking to introduce unconventional form into Louisiana iris breeding lines. Grow in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade, and divide crowded clumps every four to five years in late summer to keep the clump blooming well.

common_name: Haile Selassie Louisiana Iris (Historic Wild-Collected Near-Black Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall so roots establish before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: Haile Selassie traces to a strikingly dark, near-black wild collection made in the Louisiana marshes and named and introduced by Dorman Haymon in the 1960s. Its velvety, deeply pigmented purple-black flowers made it an important parent behind many of the darkest modern Louisiana iris hybrids bred over the following decades. Grown on its own, it remains a dramatic addition to a moist border or pond edge, blooming in mid-spring on sturdy stalks above strap-like foliage. Plant in consistently wet to moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer.

common_name: Bayou Mystique Louisiana Iris (Modern Ruffled Near-Black Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall so roots establish before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: Bayou Mystique is a modern Louisiana iris bred by Australian hybridizer Heather Pryor, producing heavily ruffled, richly saturated purple-black flowers with a fine gold-edged signal that glows against the dark petals. It has become a popular choice among newer Louisiana iris introductions for the depth and clarity of its near-black color, holding up well through the mid-spring bloom season without fading. Site it in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade, and lift and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain strong flowering.

common_name: Real Genius Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Gold and Brown Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall so roots establish before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: Real Genius, a Mary Dunn introduction, bears heavily ruffled flowers in a warm gold-and-brown blend with darker veining radiating from a bright yellow signal, a color combination that sets it apart from the more common blue, purple, and red tones in the group. It was well received on the show bench for the crispness of its ruffling and the clarity of its unusual bronze tones. Grow in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade, and divide crowded clumps every four to five years in late summer to keep clumps vigorous.

common_name: Cherokee Drums Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Mahogany-Red Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall so roots establish before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: Cherokee Drums, introduced by Louisiana iris breeder Dorman Haymon, carries heavily ruffled flowers in a deep mahogany-red to brownish-red self tone with a subtly darker signal, a warm earthy color distinct from the brighter reds found in older Louisiana iris cultivars. It flowers in mid-spring on sturdy, well-branched stalks and has been valued both as a garden plant and as breeding stock for extending the range of red-brown tones in the group. Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to sustain strong bloom.
